Efficient Electrochemical Transformation of CO2 to C2/C3
Chemicals on Benzimidazole-Functionalized Copper Surfaces
Shenghong Zhong a† , Xiulin Yang a† , Zhen Cao a† , Xinglong Dong a , Sergey M. Kozlov a , Laura Falivene a , Jing-Kai Huang a , Xiaofeng Zhou a , Mohamed N. Hedhili b , Zhiping Lai a , Kuo-Wei Huang a , Yu Han a* , Luigi Cavallo a* , and Lain-Jong Li a*
A simple and efficient catalyst, benzimidazole (BIMH)-modified copper foil, is developed to enhance the selective conversion of CO2 to C2/C3 products. The overall Faradiac efficiency (FE) for CO2 reduction reaches 92.1% and the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is lowered to a FE of 7% at -1.07 VRHE.
Controllable and selective electrochemical CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons and alcohols utilizing energy from renewable sources such as solar energy is a promising approach to produce useful chemicals to address the twin problems of fossil fuels depletion and the environmental challenges 1–3 . However, most products from existing electrocatalysts are limited to C1 chemicals, such as carbon monoxide (CO) 2,4 , formate (HCOO - ) 3 , methane (CH4) 5 or methanol (CH3OH) 6 . In an aqueous matrix, it is of great challenge to synthesize the chemicals with two carbon (C2) or three carbon (C3) atoms from CO2, owning to the extreme inertness of CO2 7 and the high kinetic energy barriers for the formation of C–C bonds 8,9 . Copper (Cu) is the only known metallic electrocatalyst capable of producing C2 feedstocks (hydrocarbons and oxygenates) with reasonable reaction rates and Faradaic efficiency (FE) 1,10 . The highest reported FE of ethanol by direct electrochemical conversion of CO2 is 63% from a Cu nanoparticle/N-doped graphene electrode 10 . Very recently, a high FE of ethylene (70%) was achieved by using a Cu nanoparticles-based gas diffusion electrode in an alkaline electrolyte 11 . However, Cu usually converts CO2 into a mixture, where more than 16 different species have been identified 1,10 and the selective yield of any product is limited by the competing reactions. Other major bottlenecks of Cu-catalyzed electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) include the competition of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and low selectivity towards
multi-carbon products 12 . Although the Cu (100) facet in nanocubes has been reported to preferably produce ethylene and other multi-carbon chemicals, its HER FE is still over 20% 1,12 . Interestingly, other approaches such as using bimetallic catalyst 13–16 or ionic liquid mediated system 17,18 could also greatly tune the selectivity towards one specific product with the FE reaching 90% 14,15 . Unfortunately, in most cases, the enhanced product is C1 species, either carbon monoxide 14–16 or formate 17
. The high yield production of C2
and C3 chemicals is still of great challenges, which deserves urgent investigations. Herein, different from previous methods via tuning the morphology or exposing facets of Cu catalysts, we report a new strategy of simply modifying the Cu surfaces with benzimidazole (BIMH); the obtained Cu(BIM)x complexes can enhance the selectivity of C2/C3 products, which is rationalized by the enhanced formation of [COOH] * intermediate, verified by our density functional theory (DFT) simulations.
Fig. S1 presents the CO2RR performance of the as-received Cu foils, consistent with previous literature 1 . To ensure the reproducibility of the experiments, as-received Cu foil was electrochemically polished in a 0.3 M KCl solution as described in experimental section. The interested electrocatalysts are the Cu foils grown with a layer of benzimidazole (BIMH)-based Cu complex (Cu(BIM)x; x= 1 or 2), which were prepared simply by soaking an Cu foil into a BIMH solution in ethanol (or propan2-ol). The Cu(BIM)x complexes (Fig. S2a) then grow on the copper surfaces spontaneously following the Equation (1) 19 , where the Cu may stay as Cu(0), Cu(I) or Cu(II).

The formation and structure characterizations of these complexes have been thoroughly studied in 1980s using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Raman spectroscopy 19– 21 . The chemical structures for these complexes are shown in Fig. 1a. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) images in Fig. 1b and Fig. 1c compare the top and cross-sectional views of the bare Cu foil (electrochemically polished) and that grown with flake-shaped Cu(BIM)x complexes (Cu foil + Cu(BIM)x). The thickness of the layer formed by these flakes is over 10 µm on Cu surfaces, which might restrict proton diffusion, increasing the local pH near the Cu surface and thus suppressing the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Interestingly, after 1 hour of CO2 reduction test at -1.07 V vs. RHE, the nanoflaked Cu(BIM)x complexes reconstructed to nano-rod shapes (Fig. S2b) due to the applied negative electrical power.
Fig. 1. Structure and morphology of the Cu(BIM)x modified Cu catalyst. (a) Chemical structures of the Cu(BIM)x complexes. (b,c) SEM images of Cu foils without (b) and with (c) Cu(BIM)x modification.
To confirm the Cu-ligand interaction as shown in Equation (1), various characterizations have been performed on Cu(BIM)xmodified Cu foil. The single N 1s binding energy value (398.9 eV) in Fig. 2a suggests that the inequivalent nitrogen atoms in BIMH become identical in Cu(BIM)x complexes. This is resulted from the deprotonation of 1-N in BIMH during the complex formation, and the negative charge is distributed equally to the two nitrogen atoms. 19 The FTIR spectrum in Fig. 2b also supports the deprotonation argument, because the N-H stretching (~ 3457 cm -1 ), N-H in-plane bending (~ 1553 cm -1 ) and N-H out-of-plane bending (~ 626 cm -1 ) are absent 20,22 , where the detailed peak assignments are shown in Table S1. Meanwhile, the Raman Cu-N stretching 23 at 462 cm -1 (Fig. 2c and Table S2) and the UV absorption peak at 274 nm (Fig. 2d), ascribed to the bonding σ(N) to antibonding (Cu) charge transfer transition 24 , provide the direct evidence of the Cu-N formation. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) binding energies of Cu 2p orbitals for bare Cu foils shown in Fig. S3 indicate that Cu 0 is the main species before and after CO2RR. The observation of small amounts of Cu 2+ in both cases was likely due to the unavoidable oxidation in air while waiting for XPS measurements. The detailed XPS Cu 2p spectrum for the Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu foil before CO2RR (Fig. 2e) reveals two
binding energies, 933.2 eV and 934.9 eV, which are assigned to Cu(I) and Cu(II) respectively 19–21 . The shake-up satellite peaks at 942.9 eV and 962.8 eV indicate the presence of Cu(II) 22,23 . The Cu LMM Auger electrons from X-ray-induced Auger electron spectroscopy (XAES) at around 912.6 eV and 915.3 eV shown in Fig. S4a are also consistently ascribed to Cuprous and Cupric cations 25 . The results clearly demonstrate that the complexes on Cu foil surfaces are mixtures of CuBIM and
Cu(BIM)2. Interestingly, after CO2RR (Fig. 2f and Fig. S4b), only Cu + peak is detectable, suggesting that Cu 2+ in the complexes be reduced to Cu + under the negative voltage applied for CO2RR. However, the exact pathway of the reduction (whether Cu 0 state and re-oxidation is involved) remains unclear without in situ characterization.
Fig. 2. Spectroscopic analysis of Cu(BIM)x-coated Cu foils. (a) Only one N 1s binding energy value is shown, indicating the two nitrogen atoms in Cu(BIM)x complex are identical. The narrowed FWHM (compared with BIMH) also suggests the formation of Cu-N bond. (b) Missing of N-H bond information implies the interaction between Cu and N. (c,d) Direct observation of Cu-N bonds through Raman and UV-vis spectra. (e) Cu(I) and Cu(II) cations are characterized through XPS, indicating the formation of two different Cu-ligands complexes on Cu surfaces. (f) After CO2RR, only Cu + is detectable, suggesting that CuBIM is the species remained on Cu surfaces.
Fig. 3a shows the CO2RR catalytic performance of a bare Cu foil at various potentials, where only C0 (i.e. H2) and C1 products are formed at -0.88 V vs. RHE. The C2 chemicals start to appear when the potential is more negative than -0.95 V. The C3 feedstocks are detected when the potential is at -1.01 V, and the FE of C0, C1 and C2 products are roughly the same (~ 30% each). Fig. 3b shows that the Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu foil exhibits similar electro-catalytic activity to the bare Cu-foil when the applied potential is more positive than -0.95 V. By contrast, when a more negative potential is applied, Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu foil shows much higher C2 and C3 ratios in the product. Interestingly, the FE of the unwanted HER can be as low as 7% when the potential is set as -1.07V, where a high percentage of C2 and C3 products (FE > 75%) and high FE of CO2RR (> 90%) for Cu-based catalysts are achieved 1,12,14–16 . Note that a very high yield 73% of C2 chemicals (including ethylene, ethanol, acetate,

We also observe 4% of C3 chemicals (1-propanol and propionaldehyde) in the products (see Fig. S5 and Fig. S6 and Table S3 for spectroscopic assignments). The partial current density of each CO2RR product at various working potentials is plotted in Fig. S7. The electrochemically active surface areas (ECSA), indexed by double layer capacitance in Fig. 3c and Fig. S8, shows that ECSA of the Cu(BIM)x modified Cu foil is about 52.7% of that for the bare Cu foil. This observation also indicates that the underlying Cu surfaces, rather than Cu(BIM)x complexes, are the active surfaces for CO2RR (also see Fig. S9). The Cu(BIM)x modified Cu foil can be stable at least for 10 hours, maintaining a steady CO2RR current density ~-25mA/cm 2 and FE ~90% at -1.09 V vs. RHE (Fig. 3d and Table S4). To exclude the possibility that the organic ligand in Cu(BIM)x may participate as the carbon source for CO2RR, Cu(BIM)xmodified Cu foil was electrolyzed in 0.1 M KHCO3 with a flow of Ar (without CO2) under -1.1 V for 1 hour. No carbon containing products are detected (Fig. S10a), demonstrating that ligands and complexes are electrochemically stable under our experimental conditions. The stability of complexes was also supported by the similar FT-IR peaks information before and after CO2RR (Fig. S10b). To confirm that CO2/bicarbonate is the sole source of carbon, 13 C labeling experiments were conducted. In these experiments, Cu(BIM)x modified Cu foil (prepared in propan-2-ol solution to avoid 12 C-ethanol contamination) were electrolyzed under -1.05 V in a 13
CO2-
saturated 0.1 M KH 13 CO3 aqueous solution purged with 13 CO2. The 13 C-ethylene was detected by an on-line GC-mass spectrum (Fig. 3e and Fig. S11). Other main liquid products were analyzed by 1 H NMR (Fig. 3f and Fig. 3g). From the 1 H NMR spectrum, the formation of 13 C-formate, 13 C2-ethanol, 13
C2-acetaldehyde and 13 C3-n-propanol were confirmed by
their characteristic 1 H− 13 C splitting patterns and 1 JC−H values 26 . Due to the unavoidable presence of 12 C impurity in 13
CO2, trace
amount of 12 C products were detected. Notably, ethanol and propan-2-ol show similar chemical shift at 1.04 ppm and 1.03 ppm; however, they have different characteristic 1H splitting with triplet and doublet peeks respectively. Thus, the double peeks at 1.03 ppm should be assigned to propan-2-ol, which was the remaining solvent introduced during sample preparation process. In brief, 13 C isotope-labeling experiments confirm that CO2/bicarbonate is the sole source of carbon in our products.
To identify the role of the imidazole ring in the catalytic cycle, we tried another two different ligands, imidazole (IMH) and 2- methyl-imidazole (MIMH; Fig. S12). Interestingly, similar to the benzimidazole, imidazole-modified Cu foil shows the enhancement of the formation of C2/C3 products, while 2- methyl-imidazole does not significantly change the percentage of C2/C3 products, indicating the number 2 carbon (2-C) of the imidazole ring can be critical in the discussed catalytic process. To further support this hypothesis, density functional theory (DFT) calculations (detailed in supplementary material) were performed to investigate the role of this 2-C in the
benzimidazolium ring. We follow the same strategy used in previous investigations of CO2RR on Cu surface 27 . In general, CO2 can be reduced following two distinct reaction paths: i)
reaction with absorbed hydrogen on Cu surface (H δ) to form [HCOO] * , which leads to the production of formate; ii) reaction with the hydrogen from water (H δ+ ) to form [COOH] * , which then leads to CO or even C2/C3 formations at more negative potentials 28 .
Fig. 3. Catalytic performance. (a,b) Faradaic efficiencies of (a) bare Cu foil and (b) Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu foil under various potentials, where C1 chemicals were represented by tilted lines, and C2 products were notated by cross lines, and C3 species were depicted by vertical lines. (c) The electrochemically active surface area for the bare and Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu foils. (d) The stability test of Cu(BIM)xmodified Cu foil catalyst over 10 hours at -1.09 V vs. RHE. Mass Spectrum of 13 C-ethylene (e), 1 H NMR spectra of 13 C-formate (f), 13 C-ethanol, 13 C-acetaldehyde and 13 C-n-propanol (g) after bulk electrolysis at −1.05 V in a 13 C-enriched CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution.
Employing a simplified model, our calculations in Fig. S13 and Fig. S14 demonstrate that 2-C of the imidazole aromatic ring is able to capture one extra proton with δ+ charge under a certain applied reduction voltage (more negative than -0.71 V). This result is in line with that the catalytic performance of bare and Cu(BIM)x covered Cu foil differs only at experimental potentials more negative than -0.95 V. According to Bader charge analysis 29 , the extra H at 2-C has δ+ charges of 0.1 a.u., whereas the H absorbed on Cu surface has δ- charge of -0.3 a.u. (Fig. 4). While the latter H δspecies are known to react with the positively charged C atom of CO2 and yield [HCOO] * intermediate, leading to the formation of formate, the H δ+ species (usually coming from water) are known to hydrogenate negatively charged O of CO2, leading to [COOH] * intermediate. The intermediate can then release OH - to complete the reduction of carbon dioxide to CO (Fig. S14 and Fig. S15). Moreover, at relative negative potentials, early C–C coupling through adsorbed CO dimerization dominates, suppressing the C1 pathways by kinetics, thereby boosting selectivity for multi-

Taken together, the production of C2/C3
chemicals were enhanced by benzimidazole modified Cu foil in three aspects: (1) the thick Cu(BIM)x layer formed on Cu surface restricted proton diffusion, thereby increasing the local pH near Cu surface to suppress HER; (2) the benzimidazole species provided a source of highly active H δ+ that facilitates the formation of [COOH] * intermediate (Fig. S16), resulting in a low selectivity to formate (< 5%); (3) relative negative potential promoted early C-C coupling, boosting the selectivity of C2/C3 products.
Fig. 4. Bader charge of hydrogen binding to the Cu surface (a), and the hydrogen at benzimidazole ring (b).
In summary, we developed an imidazole ligand-assisted CO2 reduction electrochemical catalyst, which is composed of a copper foil and immobilized ligands. The Cu(BIM)x-modified Cu catalyst directly converts CO2 to value-added chemicals with an excellent selectivity (with the highest FE of ~77% for C2+ chemicals, ~92% for CO2RR, and only ~7% for H2). By comparing the catalytic performance of bare copper with the complex-modified copper, we demonstrate that the presence of imidazole motifs is crucial for achieving the high C2 products selectivity via C-C coupling, suggesting the synergistic effect of these complexes to copper foil electrode as a novel strategy for designing highly selective CO2 electrochemical reduction catalysts. Our work implies the selective formation of longer chain chemicals may be realized through careful control for the reactions at a molecular level.
